abstract: Fiber photometry signals combine fast neurotransmitter transients with slower changes in baseline. However, current pipelines separate the two before measuring either, so errors in one carry over into the other. Here we present PhotoSVI, a multi-scale statistical model that splits a recording into a slow tonic signal and discrete release events, estimated together. For each recording, PhotoSVI returns event probabilities over time, the drug effect on event rate with its uncertainty, and the time course of the tonic response, and it pools recordings across a cohort. In simulations matched to experimental recordings, PhotoSVI detected transients and recovered the shape of the tonic response more accurately than existing methods. In mouse dopamine recordings, it revealed an effect that count-based analyses largely missed: a nociceptin receptor agonist enhances the phasic response to morphine while reducing the tonic one, consistent with lower tonic dopamine relieving phasic release from autoreceptor inhibition.
